title: "Weight Decay"
description: "A regularization technique that discourages large model parameters during optimization."
term: "Weight Decay"
letter: "W"
category: "Model Training"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Weight decay nudges model weights toward smaller values during training. This
can discourage unnecessarily complex solutions and improve generalization.

## Technical explanation

For ordinary gradient descent, L2 regularization adds a penalty
$\lambda\lVert\theta\rVert_2^2$ to the loss, producing a gradient term
proportional to $\theta$. Decoupled weight decay, used by optimizers such as
AdamW, applies parameter shrinkage separately from the adaptive gradient
update. These formulations are not equivalent for every optimizer.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Regularization can reduce overfitting and is a common training control for
large neural models. Its effects depend on the optimizer, which parameters
receive decay, learning-rate schedule, and training duration.

## How it works

Choose a decay coefficient and define which parameters it applies to. During
optimization, shrink eligible weights or include an L2 penalty. Biases and
normalization parameters are often excluded by convention, but this should be
validated for the model and framework.

## Practical example

Train two otherwise identical classifiers with different AdamW decay values.
Compare validation performance and calibration, and confirm the optimizer
parameter groups apply decay only to intended tensors.

## Common misconceptions

- Weight decay and L2 regularization are often used interchangeably, but
  decoupled weight decay differs from an L2 loss penalty with adaptive
  optimizers.
- Stronger decay is not always better; excessive regularization can cause
  underfitting.
